cells.tense: You've got your head down on something you're growing, and you know what it needs next.
cells.ask: Do the next small, unglamorous bit of care before you feel ready — the kind that takes about ten minutes. It hands you plain proof that the direction is moving with you, not just ahead of you.
cells.core:
This is the part of you that picks something and feeds it — you know which needs water today and which can wait, and you make that call without much noise. Your momentum comes from doing the ordinary thing reliably, not from any single push, and that's why it carries.

The weight is that tending one thing means another waits, and you carry that without making a fuss. Do the next small, unglamorous bit of care before you feel ready — the kind that takes about ten minutes. What it hands back is plain proof the direction is moving with you, not just ahead of you.

cells.verb: giving steady, responsible care to what's growing
cells.place: the part of you that pushes toward a goal

cells.tense: You're out ahead of the work, writing the ending before the first line is set down.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're growing and do only its next step, then leave it unfinished for today. It gives you satisfaction from what's real instead of what you're rehearsing.
cells.core:
When this is steady, you put in the time the thing actually needs and then stop, letting the finished part be enough for now. What's happening instead is that you want the end so badly you're living in a version that hasn't arrived, while the actual thing sits untouched in front of you. Every hour spent rehearsing the finish is an hour the real work doesn't get.

What makes slowing down hard is that pushing feels like protecting the thing — ease up and it might fall. Take one thing you're growing and do only its next step, then leave it unfinished for today. That gives you satisfaction from what's real instead of what you're rehearsing.

cells.tense: You're at a door that's already behind you, still holding the tools from what you tended there.
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing you used to grow and grew well, without fixing or explaining it. It hands you the plain fact that the ability is still yours, even if this direction isn't.
cells.core:
When you do reach for something here, you put your hand on it, work it steadily, and let it take the time it takes. Right now your hands are still. There's a goal you're not moving toward and nothing you're picking up — the ability didn't leave, the motion did.

What's hard is that naming what you once grew well may pull up what sits on the other side of the door, and the stillness has kept that quiet. Say out loud one thing you used to grow and grew well, without fixing or explaining it. What it hands you is the plain fact that the ability is still yours, even if this direction isn't.

cells.tense: You're already growing this, and calling it something that happened on its own.
cells.ask: Say 'I'm the one growing this' about one thing you've been calling just how it goes. It puts the plain weight of your own hand back on it.
cells.core:
At its best in this part of you, you know what you fed and what you let dry, and you say so — the work has your name on it and it holds because of how you care for it. That naming isn't happening now. You're deciding what gets watered and what gets left, in what you return to and what you quietly stop feeding, but you tell it like it's growing itself.

What's hard is that claiming it out loud makes you answerable for this in a way that's been easier to leave unnamed. Say 'I'm the one growing this' about the thing you keep calling just how it goes. What it hands back is the plain weight of your own hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're growing this yourself. The story is that it grew alone.
